chapter: La Vida and Handy's own bands
title: Losing the music Armstrong sent
summary: The band's music, sent by Louis Armstrong, was lost on the road before a contest with Celestin; they played from memory.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Oh, we was coming from Bugaloosa. And we played a dance up there that Saturday night. We had this contest with Celestan on Sunday night at the Roosevelt. And we put the music on the running boat or somewhere. The piano player was in charge of it. And he forgot to tie it or something like that. We got into the slide there. I missed the music. And they asked him, I put it on the hood. On the hood. No music. Eleven of us. I let them out at the white kitchen and I went back. All the way back to Bugaloosa looking for my music. Never did find it. I put a hand in the paper for it. Never did find my music. I did. And a lot of that music, practically all of it, Louis Armstrong had sent it to me. Out of Chicago. He had sent me that music. Matter of fact, he sent me a little trunk of music. And I lost it all.
Who had the arrangement? Was it stock?

He had some arrangement and a lot of stock, but he had a lot of arrangements in there. I don't know who did the arrangement, but he had a lot of arrangements. He had a number like, they arranged called Boku Jack, McCarty Chop Suey, Nine In The Shed, all them kind of numbers. It was hard, hard stuff to play. Yeah, I had several more up in there. Sally Trombone had an arrangement on that. That was one of them old Scott Joblin numbers though. You know, but Louis had an arrangement, or somebody arranged it for him. And he sent me that. And I lost all that music. And I was like, I'm sorry. But we went up there, went on up there. Blindfolded, we did all right too. I wasn't calling nothing, but numbers I knew there was no customer playing. They could memorize it. And I wasn't trying to play nothing. Out of ordinary, just straight stuff. Because I knew if we tried to, you know, play something about music, it would make a humbug. Everybody would get confused. Just something we all was familiar with, straight. And played that.

And then I went by World Iron. I got about $75 of all of us music. Rehearsing that, we got it down. And we had a contest with, what's his name, William there, or Donaldsonville, Claiborne Weave. And we had a contest with, up at Pelican. We had so many people in there, you couldn't get nobody else in the place.
